item.title: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella has praised Xbox's ongoing "streamlining" under Xbox CEO Asha Sharma just days after another round of layoffs hit the division. Read more
item.description:
Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella has praised Xbox's ongoing "streamlining" under Xbox CEO Asha Sharma just days after another round of layoffs hit the division.
Speaking on the Sources podcast with Alex Heath, Nadella was asked about Xbox's ongoing overhaul and the state of the brand and said he felt "fantastic".
"I feel fantastic about the IP we have right now," Nadella said (as transcribed by IG). "If I look at the studios, the IP portfolio we have, and our ability to then take that and produce great games going forward - I feel fantastic. There's some amount of streamlining the team is doing, and Asha is doing, which is great to see."
He continued: "And then we have to invent the right sustainable business model that allows us to deliver gaming to more and more people. That has always been the goal, which is we want to be a great publisher and a great platform provider for games across both PCs and Xboxes.
"So that is sort of our goal, and I think Asha and the team have said that Xbox is going to get back to growth this next fiscal year, and that's the plan they're executing on, and in that process, do a bang-up job of producing some great games."
In July, Xbox CEO Asha Sharma announced job cuts affecting 3,200 employees as part of what she called the "most significant" restructuring the company had ever undertaken. 1,600 of those layoffs were effective immediately, while some first-party studios, including Double Fine and Compulsion Games, were permitted to go independent again.

item.title: In celebration of the 40th(!!) anniversary of Castlevania, Konami is giving away the original 1986 game for free on the App Store and Google Play. Read more
item.description:
In celebration of the 40th(!!) anniversary of Castlevania, Konami is giving away the original 1986 game for free on the App Store and Google Play.
The original Castlevania, which first released on the original NES in 1986, will be free to download until 24th October 2026, and other games across the series are available with deep discounts as we brace ourselves for the next entry, Castlevania: Belmont's Curse, next month.
The original Castlevania introduced vampire hunter Simon Belmont and his fight against Dracula while the new mainline entry, Castlevania: Belmont's Curse, follows the daughter of Castlevania 3's Trevor Belmont, Rose, as she fights her way through Paris and Dracula's castle with the Vampire Killer whip in 1499. It's slated to release on 15th October for Nintendo Switch, PC via Steam, PS5, and Xbox Series X/S.
Alongside that, a series-wide sale is running across two storefronts. On the PlayStation Store, the Castlevania Anniversary Collection is 80 percent off from now until 7th October, the Dominus Collection is 50 percent off, and the Advance Collection and the Requiem: Symphony of the Night & Rondo of Blood bundle are both 70 percent off.
On Steam, running 24th September to 1st October, the Anniversary Collection is again 80 percent off, the Dominus Collection 50 percent off, the Advance Collection 70 percent off, and the Lords of Shadow games (including the Ultimate Edition, the Lords of Shadow 2 digital bundle and its Revelations DLC, and Mirror of Fate HD) are all 80 percent off.
There's also a Castlevania 40th Anniversary orchestral concert planned for spring 2027 in London, Tokyo and Los Angeles, but don't worry if you can't make it - the soundtrack to Castlevania: Black & Red is now available on most major streaming platforms.
Developer Evil Empire - known for its work on Dead Cells and the similarly styled Rogue Prince of Persia - recently announced its Belmont's Curse demo arrives on 1st October, coming to Switch, PS5, Xbox Series X/S, and PC.
Those who choose to download it can play through the entire first chapter, with any progress made carrying over to the game's full release on the 15th October. Expect 60FPS across all platforms except for the Switch, which runs at 30FPS.

item.title: Video game database MobyGames will let developers claim video game credits and customise their personal portfolios, albeit only via a new premium tier. Read more
item.description:
Video game database MobyGames will let developers claim video game credits and customise their personal portfolios, albeit only via a new premium tier.
As reported by our sister site GamesIndustry.biz, MobyGames Professional launched in beta in June, with a full 1.0 version due this autumn. Alongside enabling developers to claim credits of games they've worked on via a verification process, it also lets users build a personal portfolio page on the site.
Speaking to GamesIndustry.biz at Gamescom, product manager Reece Denzel said signups had been "great" and "thousands of developers" have already claimed their pages.
Talking specifically about the verification process behind claiming a page, which stops short of letting anyone edit their actual credit listings, Denzel said: "There's two parts to that. One is making sure that people are who they say they are, and that's a human-driven verification process that we run in the background. When it comes to making sure that credit history is reflected appropriately, the actual way that we do credits and credit verifications has not changed: It's not changed since Atari has been involved, it's not changed in a long time, and we have no plans to change that process". Atari acquired MobyGames in March 2022.
"It's very important for us to note that that does not give them the ability to edit any of the structural information about things like their credits," Denzel added. "What it does give them the opportunity to do is to go in and edit some details about themselves that are then listed as coming from the verified source of that developer."
The feature stops short of letting developers add themselves back if they were dropped from a game's credits entirely after moving on.
Developers have long grappled with the industry practice of cutting them from game credits, even if they worked on that particular game for many years. For example, Donkey Kong Country Returns HD's credits were missing the original game's development staff and in 2023, former Retro Studios engineer Zoid Kirsch said he was "let down" by the lack of individual credits in Metroid Prime Remastered.
Meanwhile, translators contracted from firms outside of Nintendo voiced their disappointment at not being credited for work on high-profile games, too.
MobyGames' Professional tier costs $14.99 a month (or $11.99 a month with an annual subscription), but there's currently a 45-day free trial period.

item.title: A US District Judge has granted Nintendo a £3.4 million ($4.5m) default judgment against James Williams, the former Reddit moderator known online as "Archbox", after he failed to respond to a lawsuit over alleged Nintendo Switch piracy. Read more
item.description:
A US District Judge has granted Nintendo a £3.4 million ($4.5m) default judgment against James Williams, the former Reddit moderator known online as "Archbox", after he failed to respond to a lawsuit over alleged Nintendo Switch piracy.
After putting Switch pirate Gary Bowser behind bars and targeting emulator software Yuzu, back in 2024 Nintendo hunted down alleged Switch pirate James "Archbox" Williams, the main moderator behind r/SwitchPirates, by tracking his Reddit posts.
By this time last year, court papers revealed Nintendo was seeking $4.5m in damages from Williams, accusing him of having "facilitated a network of unauthorised 'shops'...that have offered to the public extensive libraries of pirated Nintendo Switch games for download".
And now, according to TorrentFreak, $4.5 million (£3.4m) is exactly what Williams now owes Nintendo.
The judge noted that while Williams had not responded to the lawsuit, he must have been aware of it given he had hired a lawyer to object to a Google subpoena.
Nintendo asked for $150,000 for every one of the 30 games Williams allegedly pirated, including The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom, Mario Kart 8 Deluxe and Super Smash Bros. Ultimate, adding up to the full $4.5 million (£3.4m). The judge agreed, ruling that "Williams' egregious infringement activities merit substantial punishment here" and issued a permanent injunction barring Williams from distributing any pirated Nintendo games, not just the 30 named titles, and from encouraging anyone else to do so.
The judge also credited Nintendo for not separately seeking DMCA damages or attorneys' fees, calling it a "gesture of reasonableness" that supported awarding the maximum copyright damages.
Last month, John Romero, the co-founder of id Software and father of game series Quake and Doom, recounted a tale about when id Software worked with Taiwanese pirates to spread Doom.

item.title: Hello and welcome back to our regular feature where we write a little about the games we've been playing. item.description:
Hello and welcome back to our regular feature where we write a little about the games we've been playing. This week, Bertie's still pretending to be a vampire, Kelsey's been breeding an army of cats, Mat's been melting mounted warriors, Marie's been a willing accomplice, and Connor's been smitten all over again.
But enough of that: what have you been playing this week?
And don't forget we have an entire dusty archive of previous What We've Been Playings, just in case you don't trust your memory any more and want to check which games you've played and see what you thought of them.
I'm still playing Dawnwalker in any spare moment I get, which I think is an encouraging sign - that I still want to play a game after reviewing it. I loaded an old save so I could continue exploring the world and find new things. And I am finding new things - I've come across some brilliantly bizarre quests and encounters.
But the most bizarre moments have been unintended - from bugs. One quest broke during review and it locked two NPCs in never-ending combat, so the quest related to them was never completed. I tried everything to budge it but nothing worked. However, when I played the other day, it was fixed. The problem was, the game yanked me from another quest in order to resolve it, which nearly broke the other quest for me.
I had to painstakingly retrace my steps to find the route to the underground area I'd been in, then slightly exploit the game using a vampire blink ability to get behind a bookshelf now blocking my way. It took hours of work; I was strangely elated when I managed it. Now to fix a broken Sacred Stone ritual that's rendered a chunk of my world impassable because of a magical storm permanently raging there...
Mewgenics arrived on consoles a few weeks ago, and given that I play Edmund McMillen's The Binding of Isaac mostly handheld, I figured it a good idea to give Mewgenics a whirl handheld too.
I can confirm I have zero regrets. As soon as I realised Mewgenics supported the Switch 2's touch screen, any spare time that I did have has since gone out the window entirely while I curl up on my sofa and breed my army of battle cats. Between that and playing Silent Hill Townfall for work - which has been an absolute blast - I've been having a great time with games lately. At the cost of my social life, that is.
The best bits of Fire Emblem games are so good. Min-maxing your characters stats for extremely specific, but oddly common events. I've got a heavily defensive unit with a sword that melts through mounted units, so they take no damage on the enemy turn but wreck them all before even needing to move again. I've given one of my archers a ring that increases dodge-chance against units using bows themselves, imagining some kind of string-weaponry version of Enemy at the Gates every time I put him in their domain.
Everything else feels like padding. The social link stuff is lovely, just a little break in-between combat for a cute little chat, reminding you about the sort of humanity that all this conflict is in the necessity of protecting. It's just all the wandering around. Yes, you can fast-travel to points of interest, but not to every quest-dealer. It's the sort of thing I bounced off Marvel's Midnight Sons for, not wanting to plod in a castle that could just be a menu, and it's something that's clearly a consideration in Star Wars Zero Company, which contains as much of it as you feel up to.The variety of stuff on offer is lovely. I just wish my play-sessions had more of the stuff I’m actually there to do.
Sometimes you need to just sit down and help a goose on its mission to spread fear. Stealing toys off a table, locking a small child in a phone booth, honking at the gardener to get them out of your way while you move a welly-boot as a distraction before stealing something else. Come to think of it, this goose is a criminal genius and I'm definitely enjoying being a chaos-helping accomplice.
I have been captured by World of Warcraft yet again, despite my best efforts. What started as a brief exploration into what all the fuss was about has become a fixture of my evenings. Evenings meant for going outside are now spent killing boars and running dungeons.
It's only a brief window into the full game at this time, a level one-to-20 slice of the full journey, but it has made a strong first impression on me. I'm a big fan of the new Skyborne starting zone Zephras Isle as well. Its flowing grasslands and towering celestial pillars make for dramatic framing, especially with the new lighting effects.
I cannot wait until November when Forever fully comes out. I do believe it may eat my life entirely. But that's okay; nothing else is coming out in November anyway.

item.title: Skyrim launched almost 15 years ago while The Elder Scrolls 6 is still marinating over at Bethesda Game Studios. item.description:
Skyrim launched almost 15 years ago while The Elder Scrolls 6 is still marinating over at Bethesda Game Studios. Even so, Bethesda apparently never considered having an outside team develop a spin-off game to fill that painfully long gap - as it did once upon a time with Obsidian's Fallout: New Vegas.
That's according to Kurt Kuhlmann, a lead Skyrim developer and the fantasy series' former loremaster, who told the FRVR podcast that Bethesda is apparently too protective over its golden goose to let anyone else tackle a mainline-style game.
Kuhlmann said Fallout: New Vegas - often considered the best Fallout game in many circles - created lots of discussion around which company did it best. Bethesda or Obsidian? "There are the Obsidian, New Vegas people that think obviously New Vegas is way better, Obsidian is way better at making those games and, 'Why don't they just get Fallout altogether?'"
Bethesda supposedly didn't want those sentiments to follow The Elder Scrolls, as well - Kuhlmann said he doesn't think director Todd Howard "wanted to create that situation again."
"Todd, from my time there, he is very protective of it," Kuhlmann added. "I do think [The Elder Scrolls Online] took the heat off… there was a new Elder Scrolls product and it was ongoing. It was creating new content constantly. There are a lot of people, I mean, I know the single-player people, I'm one of those people–but there are a lot of people to whom The Elder Scrolls is now ESO. That’s their experience with it. That's what they love. That's where they got their Elder Scrolls gaming experience, and that's probably what they want more of."
It's worth noting that the former Elder Scrolls loremaster left the studio in 2023, and a lot has changed at Bethesda in the years since. Corporate owner Xbox is reportedly more focused on its biggest of big games nowadays, Fallout and The Elder Scrolls included. As part of the company's ongoing restructure and mass layoffs, Obsidian is now under the Bethesda umbrella and is even working on a new Fallout game. Perhaps there's room for a spin-off sometime after The Elder Scrolls 6 eventually comes out, though Bethesda president Jill Braff recently told staff Obsidian's "creative identity and strengths" will remain intact following the move.

item.description:
Resident Evil Requiem is still doing bonkers business while elongating Capcom's generational win streak, but the new big-screen reboot didn't make as big of an impact on game sales as you might expect. Still, according to estimates from Alinea Analytics, the ninth mainline game in the horror series has made over $500m (around £377m) and counting.
Alinea Analytics' Rhys Elliott today reported that Resident Evil Requiem has crossed the $500m mark, according to estimates from the industry analyst, which means it's outpacing every other Resident Evil game to date and is close to catching up to Leon Kennedy's last blockbuster. Resident Evil 4's remake has supposedly made more than $600m after three years, for comparison.
Some other interesting stats: Resident Evil Requiem's most popular platform is reportedly PS5. Not too surprising considering the series' tight corridors and even tighter camera angles began giving everyone the spooks on the very first PlayStation console. Requiem's sold 4m copies on PS5, 30% of which come from physical copies, despite Sony's disc-less future.
But what about the new Resident Evil film? Did it give Requiem a push? While Zach Cregger's new reboot set a series-best opening weekend, pulling in over $108m worldwide, it didn't move the needle too much as far as game sales go. Or, at least, it didn't move the needle as much as Capcom's very generous (and fairly frequent) discounts.
Funnily enough, Capcom began selling multiple Resident Evil games at a discounted price eight days before the film debuted on cinema screens. By the time the film's opening weekend rolled around, Requiem began making 4% less money per day on PS5. "From about $284k to $271k," according to the report, since the slightly increased demand didn't cancel out the game's lower-than-usual price.
Cregger's Resident Evil did give all games in the series a bump in daily players, however - and the older, non-Requiem ones also sold more during its opening. Resident Evil 2's remake was reportedly the biggest benefactor, as it enjoyed 48% more players than normal across all platforms once the film was in cinemas. The game's Raccoon City setting and the fact that it's generally a pretty great game helped, too. Resident Evil 3's remake, the one that doesn't slap quite so hard, saw a 25% jump in players.

item.description:
Control Resonant's upside down world is out now, but Remedy Entertainment's not done with the RPG just yet. The Alan Wake and Max Payne maker has detailed some of its post-launch plans for the game, which currently include new outfits, a Photo Mode and a New Game Plus Plus option for anyone who wants to carry their progress over into neverending playthroughs.
Control Resonant's current New Game Plus mode lets you keep most of Dylan Faden's paranatural upgrades in a fresh playthrough - except for traversal abilities, which would likely lead to messy sequence breaks. "We're preparing an update that will add... wait for it... New Game++, which means you can start NG+ run after NG+ run, without needing to erase all your progress," Remedy wrote. "Do 665 runs if you want!"
An update in November should also bring a much-needed Photo Mode to the game. Remedy's worlds are always gorgeous and Control Resonant's freaky, lopsided Manhattan is no different, so it's not surprising to hear players have been asking for a way to snap in-game pictures.
"We hear you, you want it, and we want to get it into your hands," said Remedy. The studio's apparently been cooking the feature for a while and have even consulted real-life virtual photographers, but Photo Mode didn't make the cut on day one "because we needed to prioritize making sure the game was in the best possible shape."
Finally, Remedy is also working on more cosmetics for Dylan. "We've seen some... eclectic outfit combinations. You can look forward to more cosmetic pieces for our favorite former coma patient/prisoner/fashion icon in future updates," Remedy said, though it didn't put out a release window for those of you treating Resonant like a dress-up sim.
Be sure to check out our full Control Resonant walkthrough if you're currently zipping across the game's twisty-turvy buildings.
Eurogamer's Control Resonant review said it's "a more action-RPG oriented follow-up to Control, but in leaving the Oldest House it also leaves behind some of what gave the original its magic."

item.title: Ubisoft Milan, the studio behind the acclaimed Mario + Rabbids games, reportedly came close to making a Zelda spin-off starring the series' biggest villain, Ganondorf, instead of regular protagonist Link - but an initially receptive Nintendo eventually pulled the plug on the whole thing. item.description:
Ubisoft Milan, the studio behind the acclaimed Mario + Rabbids games, reportedly came close to making a Zelda spin-off starring the series' biggest villain, Ganondorf, instead of regular protagonist Link - but an initially receptive Nintendo eventually pulled the plug on the whole thing.
That's according to a new report from Insider Gaming, which claims Ubisoft Milan began working on the pitch in 2022, shortly after the launch of Mario + Rabbids Sparks of Hope. Despite the Mario-themed turn-based strategy sequel's modest sales, it's said Nintendo and Ubisoft Milan began discussing another potential collaboration soon after.
According to "sources familiar with the discussions", Mario + Rabbids co-creator Davide Soliani had considerably greater ambitions this time around, and Ubisoft Milan spent the winter developing "what they deemed the perfect pitch" for Project Goliath - a new The Legend of Zelda spin-off that was to star a brand-new character as its protagonist.
Supposedly, Nintendo liked the concept but asked the team to replace their own character with Link's archnemesis, Ganondorf. Work continued, but in November 2023, Nintendo reportedly rejected Ubisoft Milan's prototype, turning the project into a what-could-have-been. As to why Nintendo ultimately said no, the reasons behind the decision "remain unclear".
After that, another project based on a Nintendo IP was supposedly discussed - rumours ranged from a new Star Fox game to another Mario spin-off - but "between late 2023 and early 2024, conversations between Nintendo and Ubisoft began to break down." With the project dead, members of the team were reportedly dispersed across the wider company to work on other things, and Davide Soliani - a 25-year Ubisoft veteran at that point - made the decision to leave the publisher and establish his own studio, Day 4 Night.
Since then, Ubisoft Milan has been collaborating with Ubisoft Montpellier on the promising Rayman Legends Untold. As for Ganondorf, his dreams of starring in his own Zelda spin-off have yet to be fulfilled, but perhaps it's an idea Nintendo might choose to revisit in some other place and time.

item.title: Embark Studios has announced a new matchmaking test for Arc Raiders that'll allow players to opt into a PvE version featuring none of the usual player-versus-player violence. It's the developer's response to a growing portion of the playerbase apparently uninterested in hurting their raiders-in-arms. Read more
item.description:
Embark Studios has announced a new matchmaking test for Arc Raiders that'll allow players to opt into a PvE version featuring none of the usual player-versus-player violence. It's the developer's response to a growing portion of the playerbase apparently uninterested in hurting their raiders-in-arms.
In a blog post on the official Arc Raiders website, executive producer Aleksander Grøndal revealed the studio's PvE test will run from 13th to 20th October, and will enable participants to choose between the new, friendlier version of Arc Raiders and the regular, more ruthless version.
Grøndal goes on to recap Arc Raiders' origin as a raid-based co-op PvE shooter with looting mechanics, and Embark's eventual decision to shift towards the extraction shooter we know today. However, in an interesting twist of fate, it turns out many players are approaching the game with a collaborative mindset despite the incentives to kill their fellow players, turning it into what Grøndal calls the "Extraction (Don’t) Shooter".
He further breaks down this phenomenon with statistics, highlighting that around 37 percent of raiders are friendly co-op players, and that this figure has grown since launch. In comparison, around 34 percent are PvP-focused - a figure that has stayed consistent since launch - and the remaining 27 or so percent of raiders are a mix between the two. So there's clearly demand for more formalised PvE.
Enter Embark's new test, and a PvE mode that'll allow for solo, duos, and trios to queue it out. Some map conditions, like night raids and hidden bunkers, will be absent as they were designed with PvP in mind. Additionally, loot value in PvE matchmaking will be lessened to take into account the reduced danger players face by playing this way.
On this front, Grøndal acknowledges some risks with this test, saying the studio will - given the amount of relatively risk-free loot players can potentially extract with - be keeping a close eye on the wider player economy. It'll be watching matchmaking times during the test too.
Finally, Grøndal notes the test does not mean a permanent PvE mode will be added in the future. Instead, he describes it as "indication that we are seriously considering it."
It's an interesting move by Arc Raiders. The game was extremely popular at launch, and continued to retain a strong playerbase in the months following. Almost immediately, the game gained notoriety due to its strangely friendly community, a distinct difference from other extraction shooters.
Some will look at this shift - which coincides with Marathon's recent announcement of a PvE mode - as an indicator of wider trends away from the hardcore PvP extraction genre. However there's a clear difference here. While Arc Raiders is certainly not as popular as it once was, this reads more like a reactive accommodation to the game's community, rather than a necessary push to win back lost players.
If Embark does decide to embrace PvE as a permanent game mode, one does wonder how it would impact future updates, and how it might create updates with both PvP and PvE players in mind. Would matchmaking become more fierce as a result? An interesting question for the future.

item.description:
Sound the alarm! Alert your loved ones! Nearly 18 years after its original announcement, Beyond Good & Evil 2 apparently still isn't dead, according to a Ubisoft Bordeaux developer who says he's been working on the game for months.
Beyond Good & Evil 2 was originally unveiled back in 2008, and has seemingly been stuck in development hell ever since. However, last year brought new signs of life when a fresh job posting for the game appeared online. And now, after another lengthy lull in updates, lead writer and associate narrative director Rik Godwin has confirmed (as spotted by IGN) the project is still in development. With Ubisoft's permission, of course.
"Odd sort of non-announcement but for the past few months I've been working on Beyond Good & Evil 2 in a support/consultant role, Godwin wrote on social media. "I am allowed to say this, I checked."
The current state of Beyond Good & Evil 2 remains a mystery, and the overall question of whether it's dead or not has confounded onlookers for years.
Since its unveiling in 2008, we've had a flashy E3 cinematic trailer, which was shared the following year. Later, Joseph Gordon Levitt's Hit Record announced a - briefly controversial - partnership with Ubisoft which would allow artists to submit works for use in the game. In 2022, the game overtook Duke Nukem Forever in the Guiness Book of Records as the longest game in-development. There was a further flurry of news in January 2023 when Ubisoft insisted Beyond Good & Evil 2 still existed, and gameplay footage emerged that September via an animator's portfolio.
Since then, Ubisoft has continued to sporadically insist, with little evidence, Beyond Good & Evil 2 remains in development, with its latest reassurance (save for Godwin's post) coming in January of this year.
Perhaps we may still yet see Beyond Good & Evil 2 emerge from this mire. There's a strange nostalgia writing about its ongoing development; I remember seeing its cinematic E3 trailer back in 2018 - I was 20-years-old at the time! Now I'm nearing 30 with a beard. Hopefully Jade has fared better. One can hope!

item.title: CD Projekt Red has shared some insight into Cyberpunk 2077: Phantom Liberty's fantastic Chimera tank boss fight, explaining it took two years to get the complicated sequence right. Read more
item.description:
CD Projekt Red has shared some insight into Cyberpunk 2077: Phantom Liberty's fantastic Chimera tank boss fight, explaining it took two years to get the complicated sequence right.
In the latest episode of AnsweRED, the official CD Projekt Red podcast, game director Gabe Amatangelo and creative director Igor Sarzyński discussed the Chimera tank in a section focused on production challenges the team faced when making Cyberpunk 2077.
"Sometimes we're making content that's a nexus point of different disciplines - the Chimera is a great example of that," Amatangelo explained. "It was gameplay, narrative, art, worldbuilding. I remember [art director] Paweł Mielniczuk and I were sending each other emails of various different military equipment of those guns, what are those called? they go 'Brrrrrrrr' [imitating a big machine gun] We wanted it to terrify you when it came up."
"I think when we were iterating, it was two years to make this boss fight work," said Mieniczuk. "We were iterating over and over." Amatangelo added that there were "so many moving parts ... Sometimes it was too gameplay, sometimes it was too narrative, sometimes too art demonstration. It was about striking a balance and I think the three of us got into it and went, 'Okay beat by beat, let's do this.'"
In the end, said Mielniczuk a little later in the conversation, "We were doing the tank I think four times, changing equipment,the weapons." Sarzyński added: "One of the most expensive art assets I think ever."
That cost would prove to be worth it. The Chimera tank fight stands out as an exceptionally exciting moment in a DLC expansion packed full of them. Former Eurogamer managing editor Tom Senior described Phantom Liberty as a "remarkable expansion and bittersweet end" for the game.

item.title: Last week brought reports of further layoffs at Build A Rocket Boy, the beleaguered studio behind the poorly received 2025 shooter MindsEye. In the wake of that news, the company - which has repeatedly attempted to blame its woes on 'sabouteurs' - has filed for administration. Read more
item.description:
Last week brought reports of further layoffs at Build A Rocket Boy, the beleaguered studio behind the poorly received 2025 shooter MindsEye. In the wake of that news, the company - which has repeatedly attempted to blame its woes on 'sabouteurs' - has filed for administration.
Build A Rocket Boy was founded in 2016 by GTA veteran Leslie Benzies, and its first game, Everywhere, was announced in 2022. Everywhere was envisaged as a user-generated content platform promising to redefine "how players connect with one another and the digital world around them". But along the way, MindsEye - initially unveiled as a component of Everywhere - evolved into a standalone "AAA" game that eventually released last June.
On release, however, the game was panned by both critics and players, and studio CEO and CTO Mark Gerhard would later describe its arrival as "without doubt, the worst launch in history". Soon after MindsEye's arrival, the layoffs began and more followed earlier this year, with Gerhard blaming the studio's woes on "organised espionage and corporate sabotage". It's a narrative he has repeatedly returned to, even as he pledged continued support for the game in June, insisting "people had their hands on the scale and deliberately tried to shape a negative narrative around the product".
Despite Gerhard's assurances around MindsEye's future, reports surfaced last week that yet more layoffs had occurred at Build a Rocket Boy and that the studio was preparing to shut its doors. One week on, Build a Rocket Boy has submitted an administration filing to the UK's Companies House - not currently publicly available - and confirmed to GamesIndustry.biz it has hired Opus Advisory Group to act as the company's administrator.
As detailed on the Companies House website, a company under administration (which may be insolvent due to cashflow problems) is placed in "statutory moratorium", freeing it from creditor enforcement actions while attempts are made to rescue it as a going concern. If it cannot be reasonably saved, the administrator will "aim to achieve a better return for creditors than would be likely if the company were wound up" without first being in administration.
As GamesIndustry.Biz notes, Build a Rocket Boy reported a £47.5m operating loss and a £36.2m net loss for the 12 months ending 30th September. At the time, it owed creditors £61.8m.
When MindsEye launched last June, Eurogamer awarded it one out of five stars saying, "Although it shows some early promise, MindsEye is sunk by a ridiculous story, inconsistent writing, poorly designed mission scenarios, and utterly atrocious combat."

item.title: I've had an on-and-off relationship with World of Warcraft ever since I first booted it up in my early teens. I love the size of the world, the joy of exploration, the kick from getting a purple drop from a dungeon at 1am. But more and more, I found myself stepping away from the endless treadmill that is the modern game. World of Warcraft: Classic, however, reunited my enthusiasm, and now Forever has properly dragged me back in. Read more
item.description:
I've had an on-and-off relationship with World of Warcraft ever since I first booted it up in my early teens. I love the size of the world, the joy of exploration, the kick from getting a purple drop from a dungeon at 1am. But more and more, I found myself stepping away from the endless treadmill that is the modern game. World of Warcraft: Classic, however, reunited my enthusiasm, and now Forever has properly dragged me back in.
When Wow Classic launched in 2019, I was entranced enough that I levelled up to 60, and after that, I continued: diving into rep grinding in The Burning Crusade Classic. Both were largely adventures in nostalgia, flipping through old photos. Later, I died over and over leveling in Hardcore Classic WoW. This injected a largely solved game with an intense level of danger that made even the blander segments of the leveling journey exciting. Scrub that I am, I never maxed a hardcore character, but every cave I died in became a milestone moment. Every other player I saw die was a spectacle, and a sombre community moment where you could mourn (or mock) a fallen comrade fighting against the odds.
Later still, I loved the bold swings Season of Discovery brought to the table. New spells, new quests, new raids built on the foundation of decades' old dungeons. This helped chip away at the sameness that inevitably haunted the Classic rerelease; some changes worked, some didn't. But either way it showed Classic World of Warcraft was a rich field worth toiling over.
All this time though there was a question: what if Blizzard took these learnings from prior excursions into the past and ran with it? What if they stayed here, took this energy, and reveled in it?
World of Warcraft: Forever is that idea realised. After announcing the WoW: Forever project at this year's BlizzCon, Blizzard launched its beta last week. It's been hugely popular, and like many others, and I've been playing ever since. At this moment, players can progress their characters up to level 20, and already there are clear signs the WoW Forever team at Blizzard knows what it's doing. These signs come in two forms: what's been changed, and what's stayed the same.
What's been changed is obviously the most apparent, and arguably the most exciting. I've taken a stroll over to the Riverglades, and this new zone has been built with such care it's easy to imagine it has always been there, simply tucked out of reach all these years. Old roads in this zone lead through ruined towns with roots in the old Warcraft RTS games. Farholde Keep, a new town located on the coast, is fantastic work, featuring environmental design that feels so organic, I turned my UI off so I could properly admire it. and slowly walked through Farholde's front door, the music hitting just as this grand horseback knight statue filled up my monitor. It's magic that, the sort of environment design that emerges organically here, and is otherwise recreated in more linear games through cinematics or locked camera pans.
Forever's new class and race combos, meanwhile, have been done with elegance. Undead Paladins take up a major role in the announcement trailer and I did fear they'd be shoehorned into the game. It would be far easier just to slap in a new class without consideration of its impact on the world and narrative, all in the name of the new. A big glowing mace prying the door open. Instead, they've been integrated into the world gracefully. Their place in The Forsaken is constantly under scrutiny, part of the Horde but not quite, ever keen to prove themselves, and this parallels The Forsaken's own place in the wider politics of World of Warcraft, creating a dynamic that makes it works. The fact I can sit on my arse and write all nerdy about the narrative merits of a new World of Warcraft class is evidence enough of the care at play here.
And the smaller stuff! World of Warcraft: Forever is full of little additions that may not mean too much looking at the game in its totality, but make all the difference as you play. There's the fact that druids, if they manage to get the entire Fang gearset from Wailing Caverns, can turn into a snake, something rarely explored in World of Warcraft at all. The possibility that mages can decipher a scroll - a Mage-specific skill - that allows them to turn a rare sword from Shadowfang Keep into a Coldflame Saber. A secluded passage from the Swamp of Sorrows that leads into Thousand Needles, offering a beautiful look into the Salt Flats and offering players an alternative path into new adventures. All these add little stops to the wider journey; it encourages you to stop and smell the Peacebloom. Through these, World of Warcraft: Forever has done what I thought impossible: it has recaptured the feeling that there are new treasures to be discovered, even if there isn't.
Because so much of World of Warcraft: Forever has been left alone, and that's a good thing. This is not a Cataclysm-style overhaul, rather a refinement and enhancement of what's already there. All of the quests you love are untouched; the dungeons you know are the same (though some new loot may surprise you); walking through Elwynn Forest or Darkshore in Forever is like coming home for Christmas: the house is the same but there are little presents scattered across the place.
The new lighting, fog, and water effects are a wonderful example of this. I remember flying into Thunderbluff right as the sun was rising over the mountains, the horizon almost lining up with the rope bridges linking the spires. When you see that, especially with the memory of how the game used to look still in your mind, it justifies the whole game. Plus, if you don't fancy this new look, you have the option to keep the visuals as they were all those years ago. A pleasant alternative that should satisfy both the dogmatic Classic fans and those eager to see the game in a new light.
I'll throw my hands up and say I didn't think the World of Warcraft: Forever team could pull this off as well as they have. I reckoned that a Classic Plus would be good - the work done in Season of Discovery showed they were willing to throw interesting ideas at the wall - but I thought it would have sharper corners. Prickly design decisions that didn't quite work, weird additions that lessened the overall experience. Instead, playing through the Forever beta has been a smooth flight without turbulence, the old and new blending together without bumps nor bruises.
Yes, there's much debate around the new Skyborne race and how "Classic" they feel. Visually they veer closer to modern WoW than other races, and seeing a Skyborne walking around in their fancy feathered bear form does at times clash with the older models. People who aren't vibing with them are valid in their feelings, Blizzard will have to handle any new additions with a watchmaker's daintily. Even with this in consideration, I'm shocked by how the magic of the original World of Warcraft has been recaptured.
Modern WoW may share a name with the old World of Warcraft, but it's fundamentally different in its design philosophy. Modern WoW is about pushing yourself ever forwards, gearing up constantly, rather than smelling the roses. Unless you're a mount collector, or a doomed All the Things addon enjoyer, it's all about vertical progression.
Yet, with World of Warcraft: Forever's beta, the team - many of whom presumably weren't involved in the original WoW - has rekindled early magic, and proven (at least to me) that they can make an MMO differently, going back to the old ways with deft hands. All they need to do is not muck it up with the full release: no pressure!

item.title: Is Sony having second thoughts about ending PlayStation disc support? The question has arisen following a report that says Sony sent "a bigger survey than they've sent almost ever before" to developers asking for feedback about the decision to stop producing disc-based games. Read more
item.description:
Is Sony having second thoughts about ending PlayStation disc support? The question has arisen following a report that says Sony sent "a bigger survey than they've sent almost ever before" to developers asking for feedback about the decision to stop producing disc-based games.
Mention of the survey comes from informed YouTube tech-reporting channel Moore's Law is Dead and its host Tom (no surname has ever been revealed). "There is a survey Sony sent out to developers - [that's] what I was told by my contacts - that is a bigger survey than they've sent almost ever before, if not ever before," he said. "And there was a question in it basically trying to ask in a not direct way: is there any issue with how we sell games physically, or something - asking developers for feedback on killing discs."
There's no other evidence for the survey's existence than this, and we've asked Sony about the report's veracity. The news follows reports from Gamescom that industry reaction isn't favourable regarding Sony's disc-ending plans. Much of the backlash has been very visible on social media, of course, where Sony has reportedly implemented newer, stricter guidelines to staff because of it. Long-time PlayStation partner Hideo Kojima even spoke out publicly, though his relationship with Sony regarding new game Physint had presumably soured by then.
Sony announced in July it would start ending PlayStation disc production from early 2028, citing dwindling physical sales and digital dominance - characterised as "consumer preferences" - as the reason why. This led to backlash but also confusion about how quickly Sony would end disc production - a factor it recently clarified, stating that disc output would drop by 10 percent in 2028, not to 10 percent. Does this then mean there's hope for games released in 2028, such as The Witcher 4, to be released on disc? CD Projekt Red previously said it was "powerless" regarding such a decision.
I think it's wishful thinking that Sony would backtrack on the decision entirely, but I could believe that its pacing of disc discontinuation might be affected, potentially by theoretical survey feedback. But does that then mean we face a situation where some games are allowed to be released on disc whereas others are not? With the discontinuation not due to begin until 2028, there's more than a year's worth of time to tinker with plans.

item.title: Bungie has announced drastic changes coming to its struggling shooter Marathon, including a shift away from its extraction roots in the coming months. The new mission statement? Making more "approachable" experiences with "different levels of intensity and commitment." Read more
item.description:
Bungie has announced drastic changes coming to its struggling shooter Marathon, including a shift away from its extraction roots in the coming months. The new mission statement? Making more "approachable" experiences with "different levels of intensity and commitment."
Outlining its short- and long-term vision for "the future of Marathon" in a blog post published last night, Bungie said it wanted to "preserve that thrill" of Marathon's existing extraction mode "for the players who enjoy it, while creating more ways for others to experience the world and find the level of challenge that works for them."
This starts with the Nightfall refresh in October, overhauling the current player experience. It includes a regular and a free permanent NuCaloric rewards pass, recurring sponsored kit queues (matchmaking with free gear rather than your own equipment), and larger windows of access for the end-game Cryo Archive.
In December, Marathon's PvE mode Symbiosis is getting a major push as the team's "first significant step into the future", and a "lower pressure" way for people to play the game. This update also brings an experimental Team Deathmatch mode for those who don't fancy the core extraction gameplay. Additionally, December brings a new shell, a drastically different Perimeter map with new zones, a new PvE pinnacle encounter, and a fungal aesthetic.
However, the major changes come next March. While details are scarce, Bungie has detailed several specific areas it's focusing on, and which it hopes will make a meaningful difference to Marathon's health. These include an interconnected system of permanent PvE, PvP, and PvEvP experiences, a new onboarding experience, a more focused questline and narrative, a new zone, and a new alien enemy.
It's also planning "different levels of intensity and commitment", more options for solo players and crews, "more approachable" ways to enter and learn Marathon, and experiences built towards cooperation, competition, and survival. All in all, it seems like a significant shift away from Marathon's original pitch and core extraction experience.
That core, while impressive to those who could stomach the hardship Marathon offered, proved too daunting for many. And while Marathon got off to a good start, it has continued to see dwindling player numbers on PC. Can Bungie turn things around? I hope so! Despite its flaws and the hurdles faced along the way, Marathon was a bold release with many merits, its striking art style high among them. If Bungie, which is currently also making surprise changes to Destiny 2, can increase its appeal while keeping the extraction option available to the more diehard fans, Marathon might have a rosier future.

item.title: I've had a hunch ever since playing The Blood of Dawnwalker that its divisive time limit feature - whereby you have 30 in-game days and nights to save your character's family from a nasty pack of vampires - isn't as strict as Rebel Wolves once intended it. And it turns out I was right. Read more
item.description:
I've had a hunch ever since playing The Blood of Dawnwalker that its divisive time limit feature - whereby you have 30 in-game days and nights to save your character's family from a nasty pack of vampires - isn't as strict as Rebel Wolves once intended it. And it turns out I was right.
I shared the hunch with game director Konrad Tomaszkiewicz in a recent interview, explaining that I'd found the time limit overly generous when I reviewed The Blood of Dawnwalker. I rarely had to seriously deliberate about what I wanted to do and I defeated the final boss with only half my allotted time used.
The full-game experience was in stark contrast to that of the game's prologue, where time is severely limited and you do have to choose your quests carefully. My question to Tomazkiewicz was whether he and Rebel Wolves pulled back on this approach in response to public concern after the game was announced.
His response caught me slightly off guard. "Obviously!" he said, as if I'd asked him something ludicrously, well, obvious. "Obviously. Yes. We had at first a more restricted time where it was harder to beat the game, but after all of those voices, before release even, we knew that it can be a problem and we rebalanced it this way to give the buffer for the people to not fear this.
"The prologue was the first small test-field for time," he added, "and we didn't change it because we wanted to give this experience for people and show them what they can expect. Actually later on we changed the main game, besides the prologue, because we were afraid that people will complain too much that it's too restricted."
The way time works in The Blood of Dawnwalker is every quest-related activity you do costs a segment of time, and the cost is clearly marked on a time gauge. And this is the only way time moves forward; it does not progress while running around the world, or while selling things or battling incidental packs of wolves, say. Factor in that you have 16 segments of time a day and most quests only cost a few segments, and there's a lot you're able to accomplish.
How much stricter was the original vision? "Quite [a lot]," said Tomaszkiewicz. "You needed to think about everything even more carefully. But we started to speak with Mateusz [Tomaszkiewicz, creative director and Konrad's brother] and the rest of the team about what we wanted to achieve, and we figured out that we don't want to create a mini-game from it. We wanted to give the player the proper feeling and proper emotions in the main story. This is the purpose of the main story, not to create a challenge for it."
One of the ways much of your time is used is by spending skill points to learn skills, surprisingly. Skills can be upgraded multiple times and as they get stronger, the cost increases too, often to include segments of time. It's not uncommon to have many amassed skill points to spend at a shrine, and for day to turn into night while you do so.
I've always thought that was an odd design decision - why tax people for powering up? But I discovered there's a solid reason for it. "You know the source of it is quite simple," Tomaszkiewicz explained. "We figured out that if we don't have it, then what players are doing is skipping the whole content. They are farming the boars, wolves, and other enemies to [level up and earn skill points]. They're learning the perks and then they just go, on the first day, to kill Brencis." Brencis being the main antagonist and boss.
Something else I wondered: why aren't there, if you have a time system like this, events that progress in the world according to their own fixed timetables? As in, events which may or may not be available depending on when you discover them? The time system seems ideally suited to this, and there was, apparently, a discussion.
"We spoke about it," Tomaskiewicz said, "and we were afraid that it's too risky to show the player that something happens somewhere and you are not taking part in it. You are not aware that it's happening. That's why we decided that we will approach it in a different way. We will approach it this way: that you are encountering some stuff, and if you decide that you don't want to be part of it and you're just going to do other things, then we have the choice of doing the quest or event or doing something else in the world."
The time mechanic has been - and continues to be - a major part of the conversation around The Blood of Dawnwalker. Indeed, one of the most popular mods for The Blood of Dawnwalker after the game was released this month was a mod to remove it. But just because the time limit is central to this game doesn't mean it necessarily features in what Rebel Wolves intends to be a Dawnwalker series. "We are also considering and researching some other crazy ideas which can make the RPG genre different to surprise people in the future," Tomazkiewicz told me in a separate Blood of Dawnwalker news story.
Meanwhile, Rebel Wolves continues to address feedback and update The Blood of Dawnwalker post-release. To this end, Rebel Wolves is preparing the first big Blood of Dawnwalker patch for early October, addressing combat, difficulty, performance, and more fluid traversal around the game's world.

item.title: It's been another difficult week for Xbox and the many studios it operates, as a second wave of layoffs has ripped through the company. The saddest news surrounds the impending closure of Hellblade studio Ninja Theory, but layoffs have all but dismantled Halo Studios and halved Age of Empires developer World's Edge as well. Read more
item.description:
It's been another difficult week for Xbox and the many studios it operates, as a second wave of layoffs has ripped through the company. The saddest news surrounds the impending closure of Hellblade studio Ninja Theory, but layoffs have all but dismantled Halo Studios and halved Age of Empires developer World's Edge as well.
However, that's not all that happened. Besides the layoffs, there's been notable restructuring of the Xbox division, effectively re-delegating the management of studios away from Xbox directly, to either Bethesda or Activision - publishing operations Xbox owns. Obsidian moved to Bethesda, while Rare, World's Edge and Halo moved to Activision.
Since the news, there's been an outpouring of concern from the communities of each studio's games, some wondering if Activision will operate these new businesses as it does Call of Duty, and more aggressively monetise their games, while others are questioning whether Obsidian will now have freedom to make anything that isn't Bethesda-related.
Ninja Theory still hasn't said anything publicly related to the studio's impending closure, nor have any of the key figures there. Understandably, the sentiment on the Hellblade subreddit is sad, with an announcement post labelling it "devastating".
"The whiplash is what really frustrates me," that post read. "Three months ago, they were on stage at the Xbox reveal for Senua. What's the point of showcasing a brand-new game if you're going to shut down the studio who made it?" Responses to this suggested Xbox did it to make Ninja Theory seem as appealing as possible to any possible buyers of the studio.
Other posts highlight how Ninja Theory was "one of the few arthouse developers in the triple-A space", and that perhaps this signals Xbox's move away from "ambitious, artistic and less mainstream titles" and towards "games with calculated sales potential". However, some questioned how successful the Hellblade series actually was, and highlighted Ninja Theory's foray into hero shooters with 2020's ill-fated Bleeding Edge.
"It genuinely breaks my heart," wrote another redditor, revealing a touching personal anecdote related to the studio. "I once reached out to Ninja Theory pre-Microsoft acquisition because I wanted to get a Hellblade tattoo, with runes inspired by music from the game, but wanted to make sure they were accurate. NT got back to me within days, said they didn't have an expert on-staff who knew [the ancient alphabet] Elder Futhark but gave me the contact for the Oxford professor they consulted [with] for the game. She was so detailed in her answer and I got my tattoo with an awesome story. And Melina [Juergens, the actor who portrayed Senua] was the first person on [Instagram] to like my post showing it off!
"They've always been so human throughout the production and you could tell they took pride in their work ... I can't believe I'm referring to them in past tense like a lost loved one, but it doesn't feel too far off. Yeah... this one hurts."
Obsidian also hasn't said anything publicly following the restructuring, though its new overlord Bethesda has promised Obsidian's "creative identity and strengths" will be retained. The big question here is whether Obsidian has scope to work on anything that isn't the new Fallout game announced by Xbox earlier this year.
"Even as a huge fan of Bethesda, I don't see good coming from this," wrote one observer on the Outer Worlds subreddit - a series that could be impacted by the move. But others were at least optimistic about the series' immediate future, noting the Premium Edition for The Outer Worlds 2 came with a DLC pass for two add-ons, which haven't arrived yet. "Do you really think that Obsidian would just cancel DLC that people paid for?" they said.
The other game Obsidian currently operates is Grounded 2, which is in early access and expanding this year with the Into the Abyss update. As many people highlighted on the game's subreddit: "People underestimate how well Grounded does for Xbox and how huge of a franchise it actually is. It's gonna stay safe." Indeed, Xbox alluded to such in its memo this week, saying Obsidian "will continue with its current projects, including Grounded".
That leaves Avowed and Pillars of Eternity - games based in the same world. Unfortunately, Obsidian has said previously that Avowed missed sales targets, which doesn't bode well. And with Xbox developing Fable and a new Elder Scrolls game, it's hard to see where a new Avowed fantasy RPG would fit in. "Does this mean Obsidian is just gonna be the Fallout Spin-off Team like id Software with Doom or...?" One Fallout subredditor asked, open-endedly.
The decision to merge Forza developers Playground Games and Turn 10 hasn't caused much commotion, partly because, as many people on the Forza subreddits point out, Turn 10 doesn't seem to exist in a meaningful capacity any more.
"If anything this means Turn 10 and Motorsport is done," stated a member of the Forza Horizon subreddit. "The only thing Turn 10 is going to do (right now) is possibly help Horizon 6's expansions (maps, car models, porting stuff from Motorsport that isn't in the Horizon series yet) while Playground finishes up Fable."
It's a sad state of affairs for some. "The latest Motorsport was a disappointment," lamented one redditor, "but as a long time Motorsport fan, this is incredibly sad. I hope they at least port the tracks from Motorsport over to Horizon. I'm going to miss trying to shave tenths of a second off of lap times."
As far as Age of Empires 2: Definitive Edition support is concerned, some in the community fear it's the end after developer World's End suffered substantial layoffs this week. "RIP AOE2 1999-2026," one subredditor succinctly put it. "Well, it was fun while it lasted," said another.
On the Sea of Thieves subreddit, people shared edited and animated GIFs from the film Titanic to insinuate a sinking ship, and sentiments such as: "I'm teetering between 'Oh God not CoD' and 'Could they really do worse?'" And it's this latter point about Sea of Thieves' currently unfavourable state that seems to dominate.
"We already had Gears, Halo and Rare games skin in SoT," another person pointed out.
Rare hasn't said anything publicly in response to the Xbox restructuring yet, but there don't appear to be any layoffs - or layoffs in noticeable quantities - connected to the company. This suggests it's working on something Microsoft values, the question being: what, exactly? Rare's fantastical forest multiplayer game Everwild was cancelled a year ago, and recent leaks have suggested we might be looking at an impending Sea of Thieves spin-off or sequel.
A heavy week, then, and again, our thoughts are with everyone affected by the Xbox layoffs.

Naturally, though, Rockstar says nothing about it on its website, nor does it make any harmless jokes about them being used in this manner, either - though the mirror does apparently allow you to "Reflect on your life choices".
This is a pretty funny gag to include within a collector's package for an adult game based in Florida / Miami. Though that statue crocodile statue looks like a dandy little desk piece, one you wouldn't have to worry about your loved ones finding left around the house.
